Yayoi Kusama (Japanese: 草間 彌生, Hepburn: Kusama Yayoi, 22 March 1929, 14 August 2026) was a Japanese artist who worked primarily in sculpture and installation. She was also active in painting, performance art, video art, fashion, poetry, and fiction.

Rooted in conceptual art, her work incorporates elements of feminist art, minimalism, surrealism, art brut, pop art, and abstract expressionism, and is infused with autobiographical, psychological, and sexual themes.

Acknowledged as one of the most important artists to emerge from Japan, she was among the world's top-selling female artists, ranking 19th on Sotheby's 2023 list of the top 50 artists. Her work influenced her contemporaries, including Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.
Raised in Matsumoto, Kusama trained for a year at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in the traditional Japanese painting style nihonga.

Drawn to European and American avant-garde movements, particularly abstract expressionism, she moved to New York City in 1958 and was a part of the New York avant-garde scene throughout the 1960s, especially in the pop art movement.

Embracing the rise of the hippie counterculture of the late 1960s, she came to public attention when she organized a series of happenings in which nude participants were painted with brightly colored polka dots.
Although her work was largely overlooked during the 1970s, critical and popular interest revived in the late 1980s, leading to major retrospectives and permanent installations at museums worldwide.
Open about her struggles with mental illness, Kusama voluntarily resided in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital from 1977 until her death, crediting art as her primary means of coping with her condition.
"I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art", she told an interviewer in 2012.
Life and career
Early life: 1929, 1949

Yayoi Kusama was born on 22 March 1929 in Matsumoto, Nagano. Born into a merchant family that owned a plant nursery and seed farm, Kusama began drawing pumpkins in elementary school and depicting imagery from her visual hallucinations, motifs that would later define her career.

Her mother was not supportive of her creative endeavors, Kusama would rush to finish her art because her mother would take it away to discourage her. Her mother was physically abusive, and she remembered her father as "the type who would play around, who would womanize a lot".

She said her mother would often send her to spy on her father's extramarital affairs, which instilled in her a lifelong aversion to sexuality, particularly the male body and the phallus: "I don't like sex. I had an obsession with sex. When I was a child, my father had lovers and I experienced seeing him.

My mother sent me to spy on him. I didn't want to have sex with anyone for years... " Pumpkins, which became a central motif in her art, first captivated her during a childhood visit to a large seed-harvesting ground with her grandfather.
She recalled being "enchanted by their charming and winsome form" and their "generous unpretentiousness", despite their humble status.

At age ten, Kusama began experiencing vivid hallucinations that she described as "flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots", including talking flowers and fabric patterns that appeared to come to life, multiply, and engulf her.

Art became her refuge from both her family and her hallucinations, and she translated this sensation of being absorbed into her surroundings into an artistic practice she termed "self-obliteration". She also cited the smooth white stones covering the riverbed near her family home as a formative influence on her lifelong fixation with dots.
During the Pacific War, when Kusama was 13, she was sent to work in a military factory where she was tasked with making parachutes for the Imperial Japanese Army.

Discussing her time in the factory, she recalled spending her adolescence "in closed darkness", though she constantly heard air raid sirens and saw American B-29s flying overhead during the day. While attending Nagano Prefectural Matsumoto Arigasaki High School, the wartime deprivation shaped her enduring commitment to personal and creative freedom.

She went on to study nihonga painting at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in 1948. Frustrated with this distinctly Japanese style, she became interested in the European and American avant-garde, staging several solo exhibitions of her paintings in Matsumoto and Tokyo in the 1950s.
Early success in Japan: 1950, 1956

By 1950, she was depicting abstract natural forms in watercolor, gouache, and oil paint, primarily on paper. She began covering surfaces, walls, floors, canvases, and later household objects and nude assistants, with the polka dots that became her signature motif. She held her first solo exhibition in Matsumoto in 1952.

The earliest recorded work in which she incorporated these dots was a drawing in 1939 at age 10, in which the image of a Japanese woman in a kimono, presumed to be the artist's mother, is covered and obliterated by spots.
1 m) in length, which she covered entirely in rhythmic sequences of nets and dots alluding to her hallucinatory visions.

Although never officially affiliated with Surrealism, Kusama engaged with the movement in early gouaches such as A Circus Rider's Dream (1955) and corresponded with poet-critic Shūzō Takiguchi, a leading proponent of Surrealism in Japan.

One day I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows, and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe.

I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness. As I realised it was actually happening and not just in my imagination, I was frightened.

I knew I had to run away lest I should be deprived of my life by the spell of the red flowers. I ran desperately up the stairs. The steps below me began to fall apart and I fell down the stairs spraining my ankle.
New York City: 1957, 1972

After exhibiting in Matsumoto and Tokyo, Kusama left Japan for the United States in 1957 at the age of 28, finding Japanese society "too small, too servile, too feudalistic, and too scornful of women". Before leaving Japan, she destroyed many of her early works.

She remained in Seattle for a year, holding an exhibition of paintings at the Zoe Dusanne Gallery, before relocating to New York City, having corresponded with Georgia O'Keeffe to seek advice on entering the city's art world. Arriving in New York City in 1958, she developed her signature Infinity Nets paintings and early soft sculptures.

She achieved critical acclaim with her 1959 solo exhibition at the Brata Gallery and subsequently pioneered body-art performances and happenings. In the United States, she quickly established a reputation as a leading figure in the avant-garde and drew praise from anarchist art critic Herbert Read.

In 1961, she moved her studio into the same building as Donald Judd and sculptor Eva Hesse, Hesse became a close friend. In the early 1960s, Kusama began creating 'Accumulation' soft sculptures by covering everyday objects, such as ladders, shoes, and chairs, with sewn white phallic protrusions.

Despite the painstaking intricacy of her works on paper and sculptures, she produced them rapidly and in large quantities, establishing a prolific work ethic that she maintained throughout her life. She also cultivated her public persona, routinely having herself photographed alongside new pieces and appearing in public in signature bob wigs and avant-garde attire.

In June 1963, one of Kusama's soft sculpture pieces, a couch covered with phallus-like protrusions she had sewn, was exhibited at the Green Gallery. The same exhibition included a papier-mâché piece by Claes Oldenburg, who had not previously worked in soft sculpture.

Kusama's couch drew significant critical attention, and by September Oldenburg was exhibiting his own sewn soft sculptures, several of which closely resembled Kusama's, Oldenburg's wife, Patty Mucha, apologized to Kusama at the opening.
